passage: So the school podcast asked me to talk about doubt, and here goes. Around fifteen, namaz stopped feeling like anything. I stood, bowed, repeated the words and felt nothing, and I was scared that meant something was wrong with me. I told my friend Jomon first, after cricket practice. He didn't panic. He said, "You're allowed to wonder." It took me two more months to tell Abbu. I picked a Sunday, when he was calm. I said, "Abbu, I'm not sure I believe the way you do. I still love you, and I'll come for Eid and sit with the family." He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "I need time. But you're my son." I haven't stopped being kind to him, and he hasn't stopped saving me the first plate of biryani. It's slow, but it's ours. Rafiq

qa.q: When did Rafiq tell Abbu about the doubts?
qa.a: Rafiq chose a Sunday, when Abbu was calm.

qa.q: What was Rafiq afraid of when namaz stopped feeling like anything?
qa.a: Rafiq was scared that something was wrong, and afraid of hurting Abbu by saying it.

qa.q: Which choice by Rafiq helped the family adjust?
qa.a: Rafiq picked a calm Sunday and spoke respectfully, saying he still loves Abbu and will come for Eid and sit with the family.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt hearing this?
qa.a: Probably hurt and unsettled, since he was quiet for a long time and asked for time. Yet he also said, "you're my son," which shows love.

grounding: A teenager finds prayers losing meaning, fears hurting a parent, and says so with respectful words and continued kindness.

passage: My brother Karthik, sixteen, used to be first at the puja room every morning, ringing the little bell. Around March I noticed he had stopped. He'd stand at the door for a second and then go to the kitchen. Amma noticed too and grew quiet. One evening Karthik sat on the sofa beside Amma and said, "Amma, the puja doesn't mean what it used to. I don't want to fake it. But I'm not angry at anyone, and I'll always eat the prasad and help with Diwali." Amma looked at the diya for a long while. Then she said, "Will you at least fold the flowers with me on Sundays?" He nodded. I can't say what he feels inside. But he has been making her tea every morning since. Sharmila

qa.q: What did Amma ask Karthik to do on Sundays?
qa.a: Amma asked Karthik to fold the flowers with her on Sundays.

qa.q: What might Karthik be feeling as he tells Amma the puja doesn't mean what it used to?
qa.a: Karthik is probably nervous and afraid of hurting Amma, and honest about his doubt. He says he does not want to fake it and is not angry.

qa.q: Which choice by Karthik helped Amma accept the change?
qa.a: Karthik spoke honestly and gently, promised to keep eating the prasad and helping with Diwali, and made her tea every morning.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt as she looked at the diya for a long while?
qa.a: Probably hurt and thoughtful. Her request about the flowers suggests she wanted to keep some closeness with Karthik.

grounding: A teenager finds puja losing meaning and fears hurting a parent, and speaks respectfully and stays kind, seen by a sibling.

passage: The shehnai was so loud in the wedding hall that Zubin, fifteen, could hardly hear his great-aunt, but he heard enough. "No God, no prayer, no shame in you," she said, wagging a finger. "Children without belief go astray." A cousin snickered. Zubin's face went hot. The baraat was due in ten minutes and the whole family was rushing. He didn't argue. He lifted a heavy tray of sweets from an old uncle's arms and carried it to the mandap, then fetched water for the musicians. Urmila, his cousin, caught up with him behind a pillar, her bangles clinking. "That wasn't fair. I saw you helping everyone." "I just think it's honest to say I don't know," Zubin said quietly. "You should tell her that yourself, kindly," Urmila said. "I'll sit with you when you do."

qa.q: What did Zubin carry to the mandap?
qa.a: Zubin carried a heavy tray of sweets to the mandap.

qa.q: How does Zubin feel after his great-aunt's remark, and what shows it?
qa.a: Zubin feels ashamed and stung. His face goes hot, and he does not argue, only quietly goes to help.

qa.q: Which choice by Zubin showed that values do not depend on belief?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, Zubin lifted the tray of sweets from the old uncle and fetched water for the musicians, helping people kindly.

qa.q: How does Urmila see what happened?
qa.a: Urmila sees it as unfair. She saw Zubin helping everyone, and she offers to sit with him when he explains himself kindly to his great-aunt.

grounding: A teenager who does not follow any religion is told by a relative that he will go astray, and shows kindness and honesty instead of shame.

passage: At the canteen in their Delhi school, Pranav pointed his samosa at Pankaj. "You don't believe in anything? Then you're lost, yaar. No God means no morals." A few classmates laughed. Pankaj, fifteen, felt heat in his ears. He said, "I'm not lost. I just don't believe in a god. I still think you shouldn't steal or hurt people." Pranav rolled his eyes. That afternoon, when Pranav dropped his wallet in the corridor, Pankaj ran after him to return it and said nothing more about it. At home that night Pankaj told his father, who put down the newspaper. "Honest thinking is nothing to be ashamed of," he said. "And nobody gets to call you a lesser person for it." Pankaj slept better that night.

qa.q: What did Pankaj do when Pranav dropped his wallet?
qa.a: Pankaj ran after Pranav to return the wallet and said nothing more about it.

qa.q: How does Pankaj feel when Pranav calls him lost, and what shows it?
qa.a: Pankaj feels embarrassed and stung. Heat rises in his ears, but he still answers calmly.

qa.q: What turning point helped Pankaj feel better that night?
qa.a: Pankaj told his father, who said that honest thinking is nothing to be ashamed of and that nobody may call him a lesser person for it.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt when Pankaj returned the wallet?
qa.a: Probably surprised, since the classmate he had mocked had just been kind, which shows conduct can matter more than belief.

grounding: A teenager who does not follow any religion is called lost by a classmate, shows kindness and honesty in conduct, and is supported by a parent.

passage: Dolma and I share a hostel room, so I saw a lot of this. She lights a small butter lamp every morning and turns her prayer beads in the corridor before class. Some boys in the common room started calling her "superstitious" and asking if her lamp cured exams. I watched her go quiet and put the beads in her pocket. I can't say what she felt, though she skipped the common room for a week. Then Rahul, who has said openly that he doesn't believe in any gods, sat next to her and asked, "What do you say when you turn them?" Dolma explained, a little shy. He nodded and said, "I don't share it, but I get why it matters to you." The next morning she took out the beads in the corridor again. Neelam

qa.q: What does Dolma do every morning?
qa.a: Dolma lights a small butter lamp every morning and turns her prayer beads in the corridor before class.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been feeling when she put the beads in her pocket?
qa.a: Dolma was probably hurt and self-conscious after being called superstitious, though Neelam cannot be sure what she felt inside.

qa.q: Which choice by Rahul changed things for Dolma?
qa.a: Rahul asked politely what she says when she turns the beads and listened, saying he doesn't share it but understands why it matters.

qa.q: How might Rahul see Dolma's prayer beads?
qa.a: As something he does not share but can respect. He asked what she says when she turns them and told her he gets why it matters to her.

grounding: A young person from a devout family is teased as superstitious, and a non-believing peer shows that respect can run in both directions.

passage: Monday. In the college canteen, three classmates laughed at Rekha, who fasts on Thursdays and wears a tulsi mala. "Still into that old stuff? So backward." Rekha smiled thinly and left her tea half finished. Wednesday. Rekha's friend Sunaina, who doesn't believe in God, sat down beside her. "I don't fast, but you're not stupid. You're thoughtful about it. Can I ask why Thursday?" Rekha explained that it was her grandmother's way and now hers, a day to slow down. Friday. When the teasing started again in the canteen, Sunaina said, "Some of us believe, some don't. Let's argue about ideas, not people." Rekha met her eye and smiled.

qa.q: What does Rekha do on Thursdays?
qa.a: Rekha fasts on Thursdays.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel on Monday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Rekha felt hurt and embarrassed. She smiled thinly and left her tea half finished.

qa.q: Which choice by Sunaina on Wednesday changed things?
qa.a: Sunaina, who does not believe, said Rekha was not stupid and asked politely why Thursday, so Rekha could explain in her own words.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see Rekha's fasting?
qa.a: As something thoughtful that comes from Rekha's grandmother's way. Sunaina does not share it but respects it, and says believers and non-believers can differ warmly.

grounding: A young person from a devout family is teased as backward, and a friend who does not believe shows respect running in both directions.

passage: Note, student counselling, Thursday. Karthik, 20, asked for advice before Diwali. He does not believe in God but does not want to hurt his family, and his mother expects him at the puja. I asked what he wants. He said, "I want to be there, and I don't want to pretend." I did not tell him what to believe. We practised what he could say. On Monday he came back. He had told his mother in the kitchen, "Amma, I don't pray the way you do, but I'd love to sit with you and light the lamps." She was quiet, then handed him the matchbox. He said he felt nervous first, then warm. I asked whether he had been honest and still belonged. He said yes. I will check in after the holidays. Deepika, counsellor

qa.q: What did Karthik's mother do after he spoke in the kitchen?
qa.a: She was quiet, then handed him the matchbox.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel telling his mother, according to the note?
qa.a: Karthik felt nervous at first and then warm, since he could be honest and still belong.

qa.q: Which choice by Karthik kept honesty and belonging together?
qa.a: Karthik told his mother gently that he does not pray the way she does but would love to sit with her and light the lamps, without pretending faith.

qa.q: How might Karthik's mother have felt handing him the matchbox?
qa.a: Probably touched and accepting. After being quiet, she gave him a real part in the puja.

grounding: A non-believer joins a family puja for love and tradition without pretending faith, being gently open about it.

passage: Tuesday night. Went to Ajji's Ganesh puja today. I have never believed, and I told Ajji last year I'm not sure about God. She just said, "Come anyway, beta." So I did, in a red kurta with the flower basket. I didn't say the mantras, but I stood beside her while she sang the aarti, and the smell of camphor and marigold took me back to being five. I held her hand. Tenzin, my friend from the hostel, texted, "Weird to go if you don't believe?" I wrote back, "It's not about proving anything. It's about her and me." Ajji whispered afterwards, "You don't have to believe, you just have to be here." I cried a little on the bus. Not sad. Just full. Irawati

qa.q: What did Ajji say when Irawati told her about doubting God last year?
qa.a: Ajji said, "Come anyway, beta."

qa.q: How does Irawati feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Irawati feels full and moved, not sad. The camphor and marigold smell and holding Ajji's hand bring back childhood warmth.

qa.q: Which choice by Irawati let honesty and belonging sit together?
qa.a: Irawati went to the puja, stood beside Ajji and held her hand without saying the mantras, and was honest that it is about Ajji and Irawati, not about proving anything.

qa.q: How might Ajji have felt having Irawati beside her?
qa.a: Probably happy and reassured. She had invited Irawati anyway and whispered that just being there is enough.

grounding: A non-believer joins a family puja for love and tradition without pretending faith, and stays open about it.

passage: On Sunday afternoon in her Delhi flat, Ganga, twenty-five, poured tea for her mother's sister, Parveen Masi, who had come straight after morning prayers. "You still think prayer is pointless, don't you?" Masi asked, half laughing. Ganga sat down. "I don't believe the way you do, Masi. But I'd like to understand what it gives you." Masi was quiet. "Since your uncle died, when I pray five times a day, I'm not alone in the house," she said at last. Ganga did not rush to argue. "That makes sense to me. I find something like it when I walk in the park at dawn." "That sounds like a comfort worth having," said Masi, "even if we disagree about why." They laughed about whether anyone is listening. When Masi left she squeezed Ganga's hand. "Come again. Bring your questions."

qa.q: When did Parveen Masi come to Ganga's flat?
qa.a: Parveen Masi came on Sunday afternoon, straight after morning prayers.

qa.q: What is Ganga feeling when she asks what prayer gives Masi?
qa.a: Ganga is curious and calm. She wants to understand and does not rush to argue.

qa.q: Which choice by Ganga made the talk end well?
qa.a: Ganga asked what prayer gives Masi and listened for the hope behind it, sharing her own dawn walks instead of scoring points.

qa.q: How might Masi have felt when Ganga asked instead of arguing?
qa.a: Probably respected and open. She spoke about feeling less alone since her husband died and invited Ganga back to bring more questions.

grounding: A young adult discusses faith with a relative by listening for the hopes behind the belief and asking questions, and both feel respected.

passage: "You really think a book decides how to live?" said Ujjwal, stirring his tea. "Maybe I do," said Ayesha. "Can I ask you something first? What do you trust instead?" "Evidence. Checking things myself." "That's fair. I trust that too, for a lot of things." She paused. "But what gives you hope when a month goes badly?" "A long run and a list of what I can control." "For me it's prayer. Not a magic switch. It reminds me to be honest and kind, even when I'm tired." "Ammi says we argue like an old couple, bhai." "You're the one who called me 'bhai'," Ayesha laughed. "But seriously, I enjoy this." Ujjwal grinned. "Me too. I still think you're wrong." "And I think you're missing something. Same tea tomorrow?" "Same tea."

qa.q: What does Ujjwal do when a month goes badly?
qa.a: Ujjwal goes for a long run and makes a list of what he can control.

qa.q: How does Ayesha feel about arguing with Ujjwal?
qa.a: Ayesha enjoys it. She laughs and says she enjoys the talk even though they disagree.

qa.q: Which choice by Ayesha kept the debate friendly?
qa.a: Ayesha asked what Ujjwal trusts instead and what gives him hope, listening before explaining her own view, and did not try to score points.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal see the conversation?
qa.a: He seems to enjoy it too, since he grins and says "Me too," though he still thinks she is wrong. He feels respected even without agreeing.

grounding: A young adult discusses faith and reason with a relative, asking questions instead of scoring points, and both end feeling respected.

passage: My neighbour Keerthana, twenty-six, has a three-year-old daughter, Ira, and I've watched how she handles questions about faith. Last week Ira came out of the lift carrying a paper diya from nursery and asked, "Is God in the diya?" Keerthana didn't laugh. She said, "Some people believe God is everywhere, some believe in different gods, and some believe there is no God. Which story would you like first?" Ira chose the elephant one. Later I saw a shelf in their hall with picture books: Diwali, Eid, Christmas, and one about stars for people who don't pray. I can't say what Keerthana herself believes; she never said. But I've heard her tell Ira, "You can ask anyone anything, politely." Minakshi

qa.q: What did Ira ask when she came out of the lift?
qa.a: Ira asked, "Is God in the diya?"

qa.q: What might Minakshi be feeling as the neighbour watches how Keerthana answers?
qa.a: Minakshi seems impressed and thoughtful, though Minakshi can only guess what Keerthana herself believes.

qa.q: Which choice by Keerthana shows fairness to many beliefs?
qa.a: Keerthana answered that some believe God is everywhere, some believe in different gods and some believe there is no God, and offered Ira a choice of stories.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see her daughter's questions?
qa.a: As welcome and worth answering calmly. She tells Ira to ask anyone anything, politely, so curiosity is safe.

grounding: A parent decides to raise a child with knowledge of several faiths and non-belief, presenting each fairly and welcoming the child's questions.

passage: Tuesday. Lalremsiami noticed four-year-old Zoe humming the hymns she had heard from her grandmother. That evening Lalremsiami told Wasim, "She asked about Eid too. I want her to know both, and also that some people don't pray at all." Wasim nodded. "Let's tell each story fairly, and let her ask." Saturday. They bought picture books on Christmas, Eid and Diwali, and one about how people wonder about the stars. Wasim read the Eid one, Lalremsiami the Christmas one. Zoe asked, "Which is the true one?" They looked at each other. "Different families believe different things," Wasim said. "You can ask us anything." Thursday. Zoe told her teacher, "My Papa's Eid and my Mama's Christmas. And Ravi's Diwali." She sounded proud.

qa.q: What kinds of picture books did they buy on Saturday?
qa.a: They bought picture books on Christmas, Eid and Diwali, and one about how people wonder about the stars.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami be feeling as the plan for Zoe is put to Wasim?
qa.a: Lalremsiami is hopeful and a little careful, wanting Zoe to know both traditions and also that some people don't pray at all.

qa.q: Which choice did Lalremsiami and Wasim make when Zoe asked which is the true one?
qa.a: They looked at each other and answered that different families believe different things and that Zoe can ask anything, instead of choosing one story.

qa.q: How might Zoe have felt telling her teacher about Eid, Christmas and Diwali?
qa.a: Proud and included, since she sounded proud when listing her Papa's Eid, her Mama's Christmas and Ravi's Diwali.

grounding: A parent decides how to raise a child with knowledge of several faiths and non-belief, presenting each fairly and letting the child ask.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: I live next door, so I hear it all. Naveen, two, has Hindi from his father, Punjabi from his Dadi and English from picture books. This morning he pointed at the kitchen and said, "Dadi, paani, water more!" Later he shouted, "Roti, please, chahiye!" His mother laughed and gave him the glass. I can't tell what he understands of each language, but he knows every word gets him what he wants. Dadi says he will sort them out later. Minakshi

qa.q: Which languages does Naveen hear at home?
qa.a: Naveen hears Hindi from his father, Punjabi from his Dadi and English from picture books.

qa.q: What might Naveen be feeling when he says "Dadi, paani, water more!"?
qa.a: Naveen wants water and is happily using every word he knows to get it. He seems eager, not confused.

qa.q: What choice did Naveen's mother make when he mixed the words?
qa.a: She laughed and gave him the glass, treating the mixed words as normal talk and not correcting him.

qa.q: What does Dadi think will happen to Naveen's mixing of languages?
qa.a: Dadi thinks he will sort the languages out later, which fits how toddlers gradually separate the sounds they hear.

grounding: A toddler in a home with Hindi, Punjabi and English mixes words from all of them, which is normal, and the child will sort them out with time.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: Monday. Ujjwal, two, pointed at the moon. "Chanda... moon!" At home they speak Hindi and Punjabi, and nursery sings in English. Amandeep smiled. Wednesday. "Doodh! More milk!" Ujjwal said, holding out the cup. Amandeep filled it. Saturday. Ujjwal told his Nani "moon" and told his Nana "chanda", pointing at the sky each time, checking who understood.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: Note to parents, Nursery B. Chinmay, five, changes language without being asked. At pick-up he told Ajji in Marathi, "Mala bhook lagli." Two minutes later he asked his friend Sameer in Hindi, "Kal khelenge?" When I said, "Good afternoon, Chinmay," he answered, "Good afternoon, Sir," and showed me his drawing. He seems to sense what each person expects. I have not corrected him or asked him to choose one language. I told his Ajji that his switching is normal and healthy. Manoj, class teacher

qa.q: What did Chinmay say to Ajji at pick-up?
qa.a: Chinmay told Ajji in Marathi, "Mala bhook lagli."

qa.q: How might Ajji have felt when she heard the teacher's words?
qa.a: Probably reassured and proud, since the teacher said the switching is normal and healthy.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: In a village near Warangal, Hafsa, five, ran from her Nani's veranda to the lane. To Nani she said in Urdu, "Nani, paani do." To her friend Mahima at the well she called in Telugu, "Raa, aadukundam!" When the school van came, the teacher said, "Good morning, Hafsa," and Hafsa answered, "Good morning, Miss," and climbed in. Mahima giggled and shouted "Bye bye!" in English, and Hafsa waved from the window, already humming a Telugu song.

qa.a: Hafsa answers in English, "Good morning, Miss," showing that she senses which language the teacher expects without being told.

qa.a: Probably playful and at ease, since she giggles and shouts "Bye bye!" in English to her friend.

grounding: A child speaks one language to a grandparent, another to a friend and English at school without being told, sensing which language each person expects.

passage: Ten minutes before the school's recitation contest, Aparna, ten, sat with her poem in her village language, Bhojpuri, trembling in her hands. Two weeks ago some classmates had laughed at her accent and said, "Say it again, it sounds so funny." Since then Aparna had spoken only textbook Hindi and had stopped singing to herself. Her teacher, Ms. Rehana, saw the paper. "Is that the poem your grandmother taught you?" Aparna nodded. "Then read it. I want the whole school to hear it." Aparna's voice shook at first. By the last line the hall was silent, and then the clapping was loud. Ms. Rehana told her, "Speaking two languages is a gift many of us wish we had."

qa.q: What language was Aparna's poem in?
qa.a: Aparna's poem was in her village language, Bhojpuri.

qa.q: What is Aparna feeling as she sits with the trembling paper?
qa.a: Aparna is nervous and ashamed of her accent, since classmates laughed and she had stopped speaking Bhojpuri.

qa.q: Which choice by Ms. Rehana protected Aparna's pride?
qa.a: Ms. Rehana asked about the poem, told Aparna to read it and said the school should hear it, praising the skill of speaking two languages.

qa.q: How might the classmates who laughed have felt when the hall clapped?
qa.a: Possibly surprised and a little embarrassed. The applause showed them that the accent and language deserve respect.

grounding: A child laughed at for an accent and mother tongue hides it, and a teacher who praises the multilingual skill restores the child's pride.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching

passage: In their new flat in Pune, Simran, nine, answered her mother's question in careful Hindi, though her mother had asked in Punjabi. "Simran, what happened to your Punjabi?" "Nothing," said Simran, staring at her sandals. At school some girls had laughed at how she said "kaddu" and copied her. Avni Ma'am, the librarian, heard about it from Simran's mother at a parent meeting. The next week she asked Simran, "Would you read a Punjabi folk tale to the younger children? I know it only in English, and they would love the real words." Simran hesitated, then read. The little ones clapped and asked for another. Simran said, "Jee, ik hor," and smiled for the first time in days.

qa.q: What did Simran say when her mother asked what happened to her Punjabi?
qa.a: Simran said, "Nothing," and stared at her sandals.

qa.q: Which choice by Avni Ma'am helped Simran regain her pride?
qa.a: Avni Ma'am invited Simran to read a Punjabi folk tale to the younger children, treating the language as a valuable skill.

qa.q: How might Simran's mother have felt hearing Simran answer in Hindi?
qa.a: Probably worried and sad, since she asked in Punjabi and wanted to know what had happened to it. She shared the story with the librarian to help.

grounding: A child laughed at for a village accent and language starts hiding it, and an adult who values multilingual skill protects the child's pride.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: Okay, so with my friends it's pure Hinglish. "Yaar, kal ka test ekdum killer tha, but we survived." It's like a secret handshake. Half the jokes only work because of the mix. My mom says I talk like a mixture, and she isn't wrong, but I don't mind. Nilesh Uncle, who works in hiring, told me something useful: "Hinglish is great with friends, but in an interview or an exam, switch to clean English or clean Hindi." I tried it in the mock interview at school. It felt weird for like five minutes and then it felt okay, like changing shoes. I still say "scene kya hai" at lunch. Different rooms, different words. I like having both. Ankita

qa.q: Who gave Ankita advice about interviews and exams?
qa.a: Nilesh Uncle, who works in hiring, gave the advice.

qa.q: How might Ankita's mom see the way Ankita talks?
qa.a: Probably as a bit of a mixture, since she says Ankita talks like one, and she may worry a little, though Ankita does not mind.

grounding: A teenager mixes Hindi and English playfully with friends as a sign of belonging, and switches to a cleaner register for interviews and exams.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: My brother Kamal, sixteen, speaks Hinglish so fast that his friends laugh in the middle of his sentences. "Bhai, aaj ka assembly ekdum boring tha, but the samosas were legit!" I watched from the stairs. Yesterday he practised for an interview at a summer science camp, in the same room. He sat up straight and said, in clear English, "I enjoy building small circuits and I'd like to learn more." Then he stopped, grinned at the mirror and said, "Okay, that felt like wearing a tie."
